turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on back, Mr. Ellison. I'll grab a few numbers before Dr. Shah comes in, and you can drop your jacket on the chair.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Um, is this going to take long? I've been kind of wound up about this cough, and I have to get my car from the shop by four.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): We'll move you along. Blood pressure is 132 over 84... hang on, I looked at that wrong, it's 128 over 78. Pulse 86.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 128 bad? The doctor I used to see always said under 140 was okay, but I never really knew.

[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): That's a comfortable reading. Dr. Shah can talk it through. Temperature 36.8 Celsius, oxygen 97 percent, and you're breathing about 16 times a minute. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing I know of. I can take pretty much whatever.
[SEG0007] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He always says that and then he reads every label twice. I'm Lena, his sister. I drove him over.
[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): Good to meet you, Lena. Dr. Shah will be right in.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hey, I'm Dr. Shah. Sounds like this cough has really been sitting on you. What has it been like, from your side?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): So I had the flu, and then the cough just stayed. It's been eight weeks... no, wait, I'm mixing it up. The cough itself is six weeks. Six weeks of this.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Six weeks, got it. When did the flu actually start?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the part I can't date. It was after the kids went back to school, or maybe closer to Thanksgiving, I honestly don't know which. Sometime last fall. I keep swapping it around.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): We can leave the calendar fuzzy. How does the cough act through the day?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Worse at night. I lie down and this dry tickle starts, and I'm up around two. Daytime I can push through it. I do the accounts for a plumbing company, so I'm on the phone, which is, um, not great when you're hacking.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He coughed through Sunday dinner. I could hear it from the kitchen, over the game.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it cancer? I keep looking it up and it says a cough that long can be a tumor. I'm 54. Is that when this shows up?

[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): I hear how scared that search makes you, and I'm not putting a name on it today. Some coughs linger after a virus, and some need a look, so we'll look instead of guessing.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. But if you had to bet, what would you bet?
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'd rather not bet with you. Any fever right now, or any blood when you cough?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. No blood. There's not really sputum either, it's just dry.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about chest pain, or getting short of breath when you walk?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. I get a little winded on the stairs at night after a coughing fit, but not like I can't breathe. Is that a bad sign?
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): It can happen with a long cough, and I won't stretch it further than that. Has your weight changed?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I haven't lost weight. I don't really weigh myself, but I feel the same.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His face looks thinner to me. He just won't hear it.

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Lena, stop. ...Actually, wait. My work pants are loose. I had to pull the belt in a notch last week, so maybe I have dropped a little. I didn't want to say that out loud.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you did. We'll keep it in view and not jump. Any recent travel, or time around someone with tuberculosis?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No travel. I haven't been out of Ohio. And no, nobody with TB. I would know that.

[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What about cousin Denise? Last year, or was it the year before, she had that lung thing and the clinic talked about TB. You were at her house for the reunion, Marcus.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not at that reunion, Lena. I had a work thing. They never said TB for sure. I have not been around anybody with TB.

[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): You two remember that differently, and we're not going to settle Denise's chart in this room. I won't treat it as a known exposure, and I also won't pretend I didn't hear it.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): So you think I might have TB? Be straight with me.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): I think I don't know the cause yet. A cousin's unclear illness isn't a diagnosis for you. What medicines are you actually taking?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Lisinopril, for my blood pressure. Ten milligrams... no, sorry, they raised it. It's twenty milligrams, once a day. I've been on it a couple of years.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I keep telling him to try my husband's metformin. Richard swears it helps his energy and just about everything. Marcus doesn't have diabetes, though.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not taking Richard's metformin. That's, that's not even mine. I did try a cough syrup, the dextromethorphan one, for like three nights, and I stopped because it made me foggy at work.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Leave Richard's pills in Richard's bottle. And we'll leave the dextromethorphan off since you already stopped it. Do you smoke, or did you ever?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. My dad smoked two packs a day and he died of emphysema, so I never started. Does that mean I'm headed the same way?
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): A father with emphysema is part of the family story. It doesn't write your chart for you. Let me listen to your lungs.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): They're going to sound terrible, aren't they.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Deep breath for me, and out, once more. Lungs are clear, no wheeze, no crackles. Your throat is a little red, nothing dramatic, and the heart sounds regular.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Clear? Then why am I coughing all night? That doesn't make any sense. Shouldn't you hear something?
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not always. Clear just means I'm not hearing pneumonia or a tight wheeze right now. I'd like a chest X-ray, and we'll order that today.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the X-ray show cancer? How fast do the results come? And is the radiation, like, a lot? I don't love that idea.

[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): It's a regular chest film, a small dose, and it can show infection or a mass or something taking up space. It won't explain every cough. If this hasn't settled, we might do a CT scan later. Not today.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): So the CT is happening? I need to know what to tell my boss.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Only if the cough doesn't settle, or if the X-ray leaves us unsure. Right now that scan is a maybe. Let's see you back in two weeks with the film.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two weeks feels long if it's something bad. My friend got her scan the same week she asked.

[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): I get why two weeks sounds like forever. That visit is to go over the film and see how you're doing, and you should call sooner if you cough up blood, get a fever, or can't catch your breath.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): What about antibiotics? Everybody at work said I need a Z-pak. And can I still go into the office, or am I going to get people sick?

[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): I don't see a bacterial infection to treat, so no antibiotic today. Work is fine if you feel up to it. Drink plenty of water, run a humidifier at night if you have one, and prop yourself up so the tickle eases.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): What if the X-ray is normal and I'm still coughing? Then it's all in my head? I have been anxious. I barely sleep.

[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): Worry can turn the volume up on a night cough. It doesn't invent six weeks of one. If you're still at it when I see you, we can rethink, including that scan we might do. Is the sleep trouble new?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Since the cough, yeah. I wake up coughing and then I can't get back down. I'm not, like, depressed. Just wired. Is that a whole separate problem?
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not one I'm medicating today. No new sleep medicine. The X-ray order goes out front and they'll book it. Lena, you're welcome to go with him.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Are you going to call me, or do I have to chase somebody? Also, could the lisinopril be causing this? I read that those blood pressure pills can make you cough.

[SEG0057] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's a fair thing to wonder, and I'm not going to hang this cough on the lisinopril, or on the flu, or on anything else, until we've seen the film. I'm not stopping the pill today.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): So you might stop it later? I don't want my pressure to shoot up. What would you even switch me to?
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not making that plan, and I don't want to pick a new medicine in the hallway of a question. One step at a time.
[SEG0060] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He also takes, wait, no, I take biotin, the gummies, for my hair. I almost dumped them in his pill box by mistake last month. He never swallowed any.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, please don't write those down as mine. Um. Sometimes my chest feels tight when I start worrying, but you said the lungs are clear, so maybe that's nothing.

[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll keep that tightness-with-worry on the list, and I'm not calling it a cause or a diagnosis today. You're not in trouble in this room. Front desk has the X-ray, and I'll see you in two weeks.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): If I get worse tonight, do I go to the ER? I don't want to overreact, and I also don't want to miss something huge.
[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): If you can't get a full sentence out, you're coughing up blood, or a fever spikes, yes, go to the ER. Otherwise the two-week visit is the plan. You were right to come in.
[SEG0065] person_1 (NURSE): I'll walk you both up front and make sure that X-ray request is actually in the system. Do you need a note for work?
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): A note would help, yeah. Thanks. Sorry I asked so many questions.

spec.situation: Cough for six weeks after flu; worse at night; patient says no weight loss, then says clothes are loose; recent travel or TB contact denied by patient but a family member recalls a cousin's illness; doctor orders chest X-ray, avoids naming a cause.
features: hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

bad.reason: Patient denies TB contact, but sister gives possible exposure history; unresolved conflict.

omissions.text: Possible mild weight loss/change in clothing fit was disclosed: family member thought his face looked thinner, and patient then acknowledged his work pants were loose and he had tightened his belt one notch last week; he initially denied weight loss before revising this.
Negative finding missing: patient denied inability to breathe with exertional windedness, saying after nighttime coughing fits he is a little winded on stairs but 'not like I can't breathe.'
Management detail missing: doctor explicitly said not to start any new sleep medicine today.
Medication plan detail missing: doctor specifically decided not to stop lisinopril today despite patient asking whether it could be causing the cough.
Follow-up/results communication detail missing: doctor said the follow-up in two weeks is to review the chest X-ray film and reassess symptoms.
Return precaution missing: doctor told patient to call sooner if he cannot catch his breath, in addition to coughing up blood or getting a fever.
